newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Sri Dhana deal unique opportunity for DBS.
newsitem.headline: Sri Dhana deal unique opportunity for DBS.

text.p: Development Bank of Singapore's proposed acquisition of a controlling stake in Sri Dhana Finance Public Co Ltd represents a unique chance to get into the Thai banking industry, analysts said on Tuesday.
"It gives DBS a significant access point into a market that they wouldn't otherwise get," said Kevin Scully, banking analyst at Schroders in Singapore.
DBS confirmed on Monday it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Sri Dhana on the conditional purchase of a 60 percent stake in the Thai finance company.

It said it had attached tough conditions to the purchase, including a waiver from the normal requirement to make a mandatory offer for the rest of the company's shares, plus additional licences to operate savings account business, foreign exchange and credit business in Thailand.
DBS said it also wanted permission to open new branches in Thailand and/or a Thai commercial banking licence.
The DBS statement confirmed weeks of speculation over its intentions following Thailand's easing of rules on foreign equity participation in the finance sector.

Thai authorities recently scrapped a ban on foreign investors holding more than a 25 percent stake in finance firms in an effort to shore up the sector in the face of escalating bad loans and speculative pressure against the baht.
DBS's purchase, if it goes ahead, would be the first deal of its kind under the new, more liberal, finance regime.
Analysts estimate DBS may pay around Singapore $50 million up-front for the Sri Dhana stake. It already holds 9.5 percent of the company.

The S$50 million figure is based on Sri Dhana's shareholder funds of around 1.6 billion baht, plus goodwill, less non-performing loans, which were around 1.5 billion baht at the end of last year but have almost certainly ballooned this year.
But analysts stress that S$50 million may be only the tip of the iceberg for DBS because the bank clearly aims to expand its presence in Thailand over time.
A full Thai banking licence would almost certainly involve taking on more Thai debt, said Lim Eng Hai, head of research at securities house J.M. Sassoon.

"The final cost may come to a few hundred million (Singapore dollars) at the end, when all the write-offs and other commitments are considered," Lim said. "But this is a rare opportunity, even if they have to put up S$200 million. Even if it is not a good deal today, it is a good deal tomorrow."
ING Baring's analyst Lim Chung Chun said DBS would see the investment as a long-term project and had been clever to take advantage of the recent crisis in the Thai finance sector.

"DBS wants long-term growth potential. They are in it for the long-haul," he said. "I believe other banks in Singapore will be also taking a look at the situation in Thailand and the opportunities it presents.
"But whether any other such deals materialise remains to be seen," he added.
